title: Algorithmic_probability
summary:
Algorithmic probability, also known as Solomonoff probability, is a mathematical method of assigning a prior probability to a given observation. It was invented by Ray Solomonoff in the 1960s and is used in inductive inference theory and analyses of algorithms.

Algorithmic probability is the main ingredient of Solomonoffs theory of inductive inference, the theory of prediction based on observations. It was invented with the goal of using it for machine learning. Four principal inspirations were Occams razor (among theories consistent with observed phenomena, select the simplest), Epicurus principle of multiple explanations (keep all theories consistent with observations), modern computing theory (use of a universal Turing machine), and Bayes rule for prediction.

Algorithmic probability is closely related to Kolmogorov complexity. The concept revolves around calculating the likelihood of an output by adding up the probabilities of all programs that, when executed on a universal Turing machine, yield that particular output. Outputs generated by shorter programs are given higher probabilities. Solomonoffs enumerable measure is universal in a certain powerful sense, but the computation time can be infinite.

The AIXI model, proposed by Marcus Hutter, extends algorithmic probability by unifying it with decision theory. It describes a universal artificial agent designed to maximize expected rewards in an unknown environment, operating under the assumption that the environment can be represented by a computable probability distribution, building on Solomonoffs theory of induction and incorporating elements of reinforcement learning and sequential decision-making.
